title: Modi Just Made the First Indian PM Visit to Norway in 43 Years. He Left With 12 Deals and a Seat at the Arctic Table.
excerpt: The third India-Nordic Summit in Oslo signals a strategic pivot toward Northern Europe — driven by energy insecurity, a $100 billion FDI commitment, and the unspoken spectre of China in the Arctic.
body:
The last time an Indian prime minister visited Norway, Indira Gandhi was in power and the Cold War defined the architecture of global diplomacy. Forty-three years later, Narendra Modi arrived in Oslo on May 18 to a markedly different world — one in which energy insecurity, Arctic competition, and the economic aftershocks of multiple simultaneous conflicts have made the Nordic countries strategically important to India in ways that would have been unimaginable a generation ago.

The 3rd India-Nordic Summit, held on May 19, brought Modi together with the leaders of Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and Iceland. The day produced 12 signed agreements spanning clean energy, technology, maritime cooperation, and defence — and elevated India-Norway relations to a "Green Strategic Partnership," the kind of diplomatic upgrade that signals intent well beyond the ceremonial.

## The $100 Billion Bet

The summit builds on a year of accelerating economic engagement. Last year, India's trade and economic partnership agreement with the EFTA bloc — which includes Norway, Iceland, Switzerland, and Liechtenstein — entered into force, carrying a commitment to mobilise $100 billion in foreign direct investment into India over 15 years and create an estimated one million jobs. Earlier this year, India and the European Union signed a free trade agreement. Bilateral trade between India and the Nordic nations collectively reached $19 billion in 2024, with over 700 Nordic companies already operating on Indian soil.

The summit's agenda reflected India's development priorities with striking precision: green transition, renewable energy, digital innovation, defence, and Arctic cooperation. Finland's Nokia and Sweden's Volvo and IKEA already have deep roots in India. More significantly, during Modi's stop in Sweden before the summit, Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson announced a shared ambition to double bilateral trade and investment within five years.

In the Netherlands — the first stop on Modi's European tour — the visit yielded a headline-grabbing deal: Tata Electronics signed an agreement with Dutch semiconductor giant ASML to build a major chip fabrication plant in western India, a strategic move aimed at reducing India's dependence on East Asian supply chains.

## Energy and the Iran Shadow

The geopolitical subtext of the summit was impossible to miss. Russia's war on Ukraine and the U.S.-Israel war on Iran have created a twin energy crisis that impacts both Europe and India. Last year, Trump imposed a 25 per cent tariff on India for purchasing discounted Russian oil, forcing New Delhi to diversify its energy imports rapidly. The Nordic nations — world leaders in renewable energy, offshore wind, and hydrogen technology — represent exactly the kind of partners India needs as it recalibrates its energy strategy.

"The war on Iran has created a major economic security and energy crisis impacting both Europe and India, and managing its impacts will certainly be a big part of the discussions," said Garima Mohan of the German Marshall Fund.

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told journalists that India and Norway had differences but should unite against countries that "weaponise diplomacy, trade and technology" — a barely veiled reference to both Russia and China.

## The Arctic Play

Perhaps the most forward-looking element of the summit was the discussion around Arctic cooperation. India, which has maintained a research presence in Svalbard since 2008 and holds observer status in the Arctic Council, is eager to establish a formal India-Nordic Arctic mechanism. The region's vast reserves of natural gas, hydrocarbons, and critical minerals make it a theatre of intensifying competition — particularly as China pursues its "Polar Silk Road" initiative.

For India, deeper Arctic engagement serves dual purposes: access to resources and shipping routes that could reshape global trade, and a counter to China's expanding polar footprint.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora in Scandinavia — numbering roughly 40,000 across the five Nordic nations — the summit signals a diplomatic warmth that could translate into easier business operations, academic exchanges, and residency pathways. The semiconductor deal with ASML, in particular, could create engineering and technical roles that draw on India's deep talent pool.

But the visit also surfaced tensions. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten publicly raised concerns about minority rights in India before meeting Modi — a rare move for a European host. India's External Affairs Secretary dismissed the criticism as stemming from "a lack of understanding."

The exchange was a reminder that India's diplomatic charm offensive in Europe will not proceed without friction. But the 12 agreements signed in Oslo, the Arctic ambitions, and the sheer scale of the FDI commitments suggest that both sides have decided the strategic convergence is worth the occasional discomfort.
